reading.rtitle: The Conversation That Ended Four Years
paras: Diego Aragão was fifteen when a scout from a Portuguese club watched him play in a tournament in Recife, and sixteen when he moved to Lisbon on his own. For four years he trained twice a day. He has never described those years as unhappy — he says the opposite, that he would go back tomorrow — but he is also clear about what they cost. “People hear the word sacrifice and they think of something dramatic,” he says. “It is not. It is four hundred small things you do not do.”

The turning point came in his third season, and it was not an injury. It was a conversation. A coach told him, honestly, that he was a very good player who was not going to be a great one, and that the club would keep him another year because he was useful. Diego thanked him, finished the season, and did not renew. “From that point on, I stopped asking whether I could stay,” he says. “I started asking what I actually wanted.”

He came home at nineteen and spent the first year doing almost nothing that looked like progress. The transition was harder than the training had ever been. He had lived alone in another country and could not decide what to study. He has said since then that the demanding part of leaving is not the leaving — it is the eight or ten months afterwards, when the intensity you are used to disappears and nothing has replaced it yet.

Diego is twenty-four now and in his final year of engineering, which he decided to pursue at twenty. He still plays on Thursday nights, badly and happily. He has kept one thing from Lisbon, and it is not the football: it is the commitment to a schedule. He wakes at six. He has not missed a deadline in three years. When younger players ask him whether they should give it up, he refuses to answer. “Nobody can tell you that,” he says. “But I can tell you that it takes a toll either way. Staying takes one and leaving takes another, and you choose which one you are willing to pay.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a youth-academy career, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how Portuguese clubs recruit players in Brazil.
To show what one person gave up, what it cost, and what he kept — and to refuse to say whether it was right.
To argue that young athletes should always finish their contracts.

items.situation: Say when Diego moved to Lisbon, in one sentence.
tips: He moved to Lisbon at sixteen, in August 2017.
The age is a fence, so the sentence closes: moved, not has moved.

items.situation: Now say what has been true since he came back.
tips: He has not missed a deadline in three years.
No date, so the count is still running: has not missed.

items.situation: Ask a question about his whole life, with ever.
tips: Has he ever said he regrets it?
Ever means at any point up to now, so it never takes a date.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: I live in Sao Paulo since last year.
tips: I have lived in Sao Paulo since last year.
Since always needs the present perfect. This is the number one error from Portuguese.

items.situation: Say one thing you gave up, and when.
tips: I gave up basketball at sixteen, when I moved.
A date, so the past simple. Watch the fence.

items.situation: Now say one thing that has changed since then, with no date at all.
tips: I have studied six days a week since March.
Since a starting point, so have plus the participle.

listenings.text: So you asked me when I knew, and honestly there was no big moment. I swam for eleven years. I made two national finals and I have never once been able to explain to a normal person what four thirty in the morning does to you. The turning point was not dramatic. I got to the pool one Tuesday, I sat on the edge, and I did not want to get in. That was it. I have not raced since that day and I have not missed it as much as everybody warned me I would. What I do miss is the intensity. Nothing since has asked that much of me, and part of me is still looking for something that will.

Everybody prepares an athlete for the decision. Almost nobody prepares them for what comes after it. I have worked with people who left at seventeen and people who left at thirty-four, and the pattern is the same in both. The first two weeks feel like a holiday. The two months after that feel like freedom. And then, somewhere around month four, the structure that ran their whole day is simply gone, and nothing has replaced it yet. That gap is where the trouble lives. So my advice has not changed in twenty years: before you stop, decide what the new demanding thing is going to be. Not what you will do instead. What will ask as much of you.
